relations.note: Hidesato donated the legendary Dragon Palace bell that Benkei later dragged to Mount Hiei.
Yoshitsune's agility defeats the sword-collecting Benkei, who recognizes his superior.
Benkei dies defending the approach while Yoshitsune completes his final death ritual.
Benkei beats his disguised lord, convincing witnesses that the traveler cannot be Yoshitsune.
Benkei improvises from a blank scroll, answers Togashi, and beats Yoshitsune to preserve their disguise.
Benkei protects Yoshitsune's company by repelling Tomomori's ghost with Buddhist prayer.
Benkei swears allegiance and becomes Yoshitsune's indispensable retainer.
The famous strong boys wrestle in a popular-art crossover scene.

god_relations.note: Shrine and folk traditions identify Seimei as Inari's incarnation or beneficiary.
After Ōjin's identification with Hachiman, Jingū becomes Hachiman's sacred mother.
Medieval cult doctrine places Jingū beside Hachiman in a divine triad.
The Sea God raises waves that carry Jingū's fleet and inundate Silla.
The dragon ruler lends or gives Jingū the ebb and flood jewels.
Some later local traditions make the sea-connected maternal figures sisters.
The game reinvents Issun as a tiny wandering artist who accompanies Amaterasu.
Jimmu belongs to her heavenly imperial lineage.

god_relations.myth: Heavenly guidance during the eastern expedition
god_relations.note: She communicates protective guidance and sends Yatagarasu in the Nihon shoki.
Watatsumi is Jimmu's maternal great-grandfather.

god_relations.myth: Divine sword revives Jimmu's army at Kumano
god_relations.note: He sends his land-subduing sword through Takakuraji instead of descending personally.
Recent popular accounts call Raijin his father without a secure early source.

god_relations.myth: Divine aid for the Shuten-dōji expedition
god_relations.note: Kintoki accompanies the party seeking Hachiman’s supernatural assistance.

god_relations.myth: Prayer before the decisive centipede arrow
god_relations.note: Hidesato invoked Hachiman before firing the arrow that killed the giant centipede.
Regional tales identify Urashima’s otherworldly wife with Benzaiten, who tests him using the box.
Certain shrines and tourist narratives equate Urashima’s Dragon Palace princess with Toyotama-hime.
Urashima loses Otohime to the wealthier Ebisu in a comic theatrical parody.
The deity raises waves or a storm that prevents his sea crossing.
Later shrine tradition co-enshrines Ōnamuchi with Yamato Takeru after relocation.
The 1994 Toho fantasy film invents a personal conflict between them.

Abe no Yasuna.note: Later fox-wife traditions make Yasuna Seimei's father.

Ahiratsu-hime.note: She is Jimmu's pre-Yamato consort and mother of Tagishimimi.

Amaterasu Ōmikami.note: Later commentators identify Jingū's elaborately named Ise deity as Amaterasu.
The imperial genealogy makes Yamato Takeru a descendant of Amaterasu.

Ame-no-Hiboko.note: Jingū's maternal lineage is traced to this legendary Silla prince.

Ame-no-Oshihomimi.note: He is an intermediate ancestor in Jimmu's heavenly lineage.

Azumi-no-Isora.note: Jingū summons the marine deity, who obtains the tide jewels or guides her.

Benshin.note: Some recensions name Benshin rather than Benshō as Benkei's father.

Benshō.note: Benshō is Benkei's father in the canonical genealogy.
Judging the newborn a demon-child, Benshō proposes killing or abandoning him.

Celestial robe-bearer.myth: The feather robe extinguishes Kaguya’s earthly attachment
Celestial robe-bearer.note: The attendant gives her elixir and clothes her in the feather robe, erasing her worldly feelings.

Celestial “king” or leader.myth: Kaguya’s punishment ends and the lunar leader orders her return
Celestial “king” or leader.note: He announces that Kaguya’s terrestrial punishment is over and compels her return to the lunar capital.

Chitoku.note: Seimei disables Chitoku's boy-shaped shikigami and compels his submission.

Dainichi Nyorai.myth: Quest for the Law of Dainichi
Dainichi Nyorai.note: Yoshitsune acquires sacred esoteric knowledge called the Law of Dainichi.

Daughter of the Sea God.note: She joins Urashima in Tokoyo and gives him the prohibited casket.
She gives Urashima a casket that preserves his youth and forbids opening it.

Deity of Ashigara Pass.note: He kills the white-deer-shaped pass deity with wild chive.

Demon king of Kikenjō/Chishima.myth: Journey to the demon king’s realm
Demon king of Kikenjō/Chishima.note: Yoshitsune enters the demon king’s domain and obtains sacred esoteric knowledge.

Dragon King.myth: Destruction of the dragon household’s centipede enemy
Dragon King.note: The Dragon King recruited Hidesato to destroy the giant centipede threatening his aquatic household.
The Dragon King rewarded Hidesato with inexhaustible provisions, arms, armor, and a bronze bell.
Urashima visits the palace ruled by the Dragon King, later portrayed as Otohime’s father.

Dragon woman.myth: Dragon woman’s petition against the centipede
Dragon woman.note: After testing Hidesato on the bridge, she petitioned him to kill her household’s enemy.
She entertained Hidesato and presented or mediated inexhaustible treasures after his victory.

Dōman.note: Seimei traces the buried curse to Dōman, who confesses and is exiled.
Later traditions enlarge Dōman into Seimei's lifelong magical and divinatory rival.
Dōman steals or copies Seimei's secret book through Seimei's wife.
Some early-modern variants have Dōman murder Seimei before Seimei returns to confront him.

Eight children.note: This second group of stellar children greets Urashima at the immortal palace.

Emperor Chūai.note: Jingū is Chūai's imperial consort and wife in both chronicles.
Possessed Jingū voices the oracle while Chūai plays the lute and rejects it.
Chūai is his son and genealogical successor.

Emperor Kaika.note: Jingū belongs to a legendary imperial descendant line traced to Kaika.

Emperor Keikō.note: Keikō repeatedly dispatches him in Kojiki and formally commissions him in Nihon shoki.

Eukashi.note: Eukashi feigns submission while preparing a hall designed to crush Jimmu.

Eukashi.myth: Elder Ukashi forced into his own trap
Eukashi.note: Jimmu's followers force Eukashi into the trap, then kill and dismember him.

Five Dragon deities.note: Seimei invokes the Five Dragons during a drought; the rite is judged effective.

Fudō Myōō.note: Seimei selects the date for Senshi's veneration of Fudō without encountering the deity.
Kunisada iconographically superimposes Benkei, his actor, and Fudō Myōō without making Benkei an incarnation.
Benkei invokes Fudō’s spell while protecting Yoshitsune from Tomomori’s ghost.

Fujiwara no Hidehira.note: Benkei helps escort Yoshitsune toward Hidehira's northern protection, without a developed bilateral encounter.

Fujiwara no Moronaga.note: Later genealogy identifies Moronaga as Benkei's maternal grandfather.

Fujiwara no Yasuhira.note: Yasuhira's forces kill Benkei during their attack on Yoshitsune's residence.

Futaji-irihime.note: The Nihon shoki names the imperial princess among his consorts.

Genghis Khan.note: Modern pseudohistory claims Yoshitsune survived and became Genghis Khan.

Genkurō the fox.note: The fox impersonates Tadanobu and serves Yoshitsune during his wanderings.
Yoshitsune gives Genkurō the drum made from the skins of his parents.

Giant centipede.note: Hidesato fired three arrows against the iron-bodied monster threatening the dragon household.
His saliva-wetted third arrow pierced the centipede between the eyes and through its throat.

God of Mount Ibuki.note: He confronts the mountain god, misjudging its boar or serpent manifestation.
The god sends ice, rain, mist, and illness after his boastful challenge.

Gods of Heaven and Earth.note: They receive sacrifices and split the obstructing rock after Takeuchi's prayer.

Gozu Tennō.note: The pseudepigraphic Hoki naiden joins Gozu Tennō to Seimei's occult authority.

Hashiro Kuma-washi.note: Jingū marches against and kills the powerful winged or bird-like adversary.

Hiko-hohodemi.note: Jimmu is his grandson through Ugayafukiaezu.

Hitachibō Kaison.note: Kaison and Benkei appear as fellow monk-retainers in Yoshitsune's company.

Hiyoshi deity.note: Kintoki belongs to Yorimitsu’s contingent when it seeks aid at Hiyoshi.

Homu-ya-wake.note: The Kojiki genealogy names Homu-ya-wake as another child of Jingū.

Homuda-wake.note: Jingū bears and protects the future Emperor Ōjin as his mother.
Jingū welcomes her son with sacred congratulatory waiting-liquor.

Ibaraki-dōji.note: Kintoki joins the force opposing Ibaraki-dōji; no secure independent duel is attested.

Igatsu no Omi.note: He serves as saniwa, testing and interpreting the gods possessing Jingū.

Ihika.note: The luminous-tailed figure emerges from a well and acknowledges Jimmu.

Immortal wife’s father.note: He receives and feasts Urashima after his arrival with the immortal woman.

Immortal wife’s mother.note: She receives and feasts Urashima after his arrival with the immortal woman.

Immortals of Hōrai.note: Urashima sees and associates with the immortals after entering the sea.

Imperial ancestral spirits.note: Jingū invokes the ancestral spirits for support before the expedition.

Inabi no Ōiratsume.note: She is the mother of Ousu and Ōusu.

Inahi-no-Mikoto.note: Inahi is one of Jimmu's brothers.

Ineyoriwake.note: Ineyoriwake is his child by Futaji-irihime.

Ise Saburō Yoshimori.note: Benkei and Yoshimori appear together as Yoshitsune's retainers and escape companions.

Isukeyori-hime.myth: Jimmu courts and marries the Yamato queen
Isukeyori-hime.note: She becomes Jimmu's formal Yamato queen and mother of his successor's branch.

Itsuse-no-Mikoto.myth: Eastern expedition and battle against Naga-sune-hiko
Itsuse-no-Mikoto.note: He co-leads the expedition and advises approaching Yamato with the sun behind.

Iwa-oshi-waku-no-ko.note: The tailed child of the rock-pusher meets and submits to Jimmu.

Izasa-wake.note: Jingū sends her son to the deity and later welcomes him home.

Izumo Takeru.note: Yamato Takeru first befriends Izumo Takeru.
He secretly substitutes a wooden sword before challenging his new friend.
Yamato Takeru kills him when the false sword cannot be drawn.

Jikokuten.note: Kintoki is declared a manifestation of the eastern Heavenly King Jikokuten.

Kagosaka.note: Her stepson plots against Jingū and Ōjin but dies during omen-hunting.

Kaguya-hime-no-mikoto.note: Later geographical and learned arguments equate the literary heroine with the separate Kojiki namesake.

Kame Myōjin.note: Urashima reunites with the deified turtle-wife, and they are worshipped as a pair.

Kame-hime.note: The five-colored turtle becomes an immortal woman who marries Urashima.
She gives Urashima a jeweled casket and warns him not to open it.

Kamei Rokurō.note: Kamei participates in comic ridicule of Benkei's carpenter-like weapons.
Later artwork places Kamei beside Benkei during the final defense at Koromogawa.

Kamo no Mitsuyoshi.note: Mitsuyoshi disputes Seimei's superiority and claims calendrical instruction was reserved for him.

Kamo no Tadayuki.note: Tadayuki conceals the young Seimei after he spots approaching demons.
Tadayuki recognizes Seimei's demon sight and transmits his learning to him.

Kamo no Wake.note: Jingū sends the heroic commander to subdue the Kumaso.

Kamo no Yasunori.note: The genealogy names Yasunori as Seimei's teacher.
Seimei accompanies Yasunori to divine an imperial construction site.

Kamu-nunakawamimi.note: He is Jimmu's son and eventual imperial successor.

Kanchō Sōjō.note: At Kanchō's Hirosawa residence, Seimei kills a frog by enchantment.

Kataoka Hachirō.note: Kataoka accompanies Benkei in Yoshitsune's disguised mountain-ascetic party.

Katsuraki no Taka-nuka-hime.note: Named as Jingū's mother in the chronicle genealogy.

Kibi no Anato no Takehime.note: The Nihon shoki names her among Yamato Takeru’s consorts.

Kibi no Takehiko.note: Kibi no Takehiko accompanies him, reconnoiters Koshi, and carries his last words.

Kibitsuhiko-no-mikoto.note: Modern Okayama tradition identifies the Kibi-subduing prince as Momotarō's mythic model.

Kotoshironushi.note: Kotoshironushi identifies himself among the gods answering Jingū's inquiry.
In the Nihon shoki variant, he is the divine father of Jimmu's queen.

Kumano Gongen.note: Kumano Gongen is associated with the disguised helpers aiding Kintoki’s party.

Kumasaka Chōhan.note: An anomalous print shows Benkei crushing one of Kumasaka Chōhan's brigands.

Kumaso Takeru, elder brother.note: Disguised as a young woman, Yamato Takeru gains access to the feast.
Yamato Takeru stabs the enthralled elder brother through the chest.

Kumaso Takeru, younger brother.note: The disguised prince enters the feast and sits between the brothers.
He pursues, stabs, and rips open the younger Kumaso Takeru.
The dying younger brother confers the title Yamato Takeru upon him.

Kunitokotachi.note: Later shrine tradition co-enshrines Kunitokotachi with Yamato Takeru and Ototachibana.

Kuzunoha.note: The transformed white fox Kuzunoha becomes Seimei's mother.
After her fox identity is exposed, Kuzunoha leaves her child Seimei.

Malignant deity of Ana Ferry.note: Yamato Takeru kills the malignant ferry deity during his western return.

Malignant deity of Kashiha Ferry.note: He kills the deity that afflicts travelers with poisonous vapor.

Michi-no-omi.myth: Conquest stratagems and worship of Takamimusubi
Michi-no-omi.note: He serves as Jimmu's chief ritual and military agent.

Mikenu-no-Mikoto.note: Mikenu is one of Jimmu's brothers.

Minamoto no Hiromasa.note: Modern fiction makes Hiromasa Seimei's intimate companion and narrative foil.

Minamoto no Yorimitsu.note: Yorimitsu benefits from Seimei's divination concerning Shuten-dōji's location.

Misukitomomimitake.note: The Kibi prince is assigned as Yamato Takeru’s campaign companion.

Miyazuhime.note: Miyazuhime is his pledged bride and later wife in Owari.
He leaves Kusanagi at Miyazuhime’s dwelling before confronting Ibuki’s god.

Monju.note: Monju teaches Hakudō, beginning the transmission whose book ultimately reaches Seimei.

Mountain god of Shinano.note: He blinds or kills the white-deer mountain god with garlic.
The god’s disturbance causes Yamato Takeru to lose his way.

Naga-sune-hiko.note: Jimmu fights this Yamato ruler, whose forces mortally wound Itsuse.

Naga-sune-hiko.myth: Dispute over heavenly descent and legitimate tokens
Naga-sune-hiko.note: They dispute which heavenly descendant holds legitimate authority in Yamato.

Naka-tsutsu-no-o.note: The Sumiyoshi god provides oracle and expeditionary protection, then receives worship.

Natsuha.note: He advances against Jingū but flees after learning she killed his sister.

Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto.note: Nigihayahi is another heavenly descendant already established in Yamato.
He recognizes Jimmu's heavenly status, presents celestial tokens, and joins him.

Nihe-motsu-no-ko.note: The fishing-associated local deity meets Jimmu, identifies himself, and submits.

Ninigi.note: Jimmu descends from Ninigi through Hoori and Ugayafukiaezu.

Nuno-oshi-irihime.note: Nuno-oshi-irihime is his child by Futaji-irihime.

Okikurmi.note: A Hokkaidō tradition makes Okikurmi Yoshitsune’s host and father-in-law.
Yoshitsune steals Okikurmi’s treasures or books while his host is absent.
Japanese writers and shrine traditions identify Yoshitsune with the Ainu culture hero.

Okinaga no Sukune no Miko.note: Named as Jingū's father in the chronicle genealogy.

Oshikuma.note: Her stepson raises an army against Jingū's faction and is defeated.

Otohime.myth: Later Otohime retellings of the dragon-woman episode
Otohime.note: Edo and modern retellings name the dragon woman who petitions and rewards Hidesato as Otohime.
The turtle-woman reveals herself as the palace princess and marries Urashima.
She gives Urashima the forbidden tamatebako before his return home.

Ototachibanahime.note: She is his imperial consort in Kojiki and concubine in Nihon shoki.
She sacrifices herself to calm the storm and save his life.

Otoukashi.note: He exposes his brother's plot, submits, and joins Jimmu's adherents.

Pufferfish attendant.note: After Otohime chooses Ebisu, Urashima instead marries her pufferfish attendant.

Red dragon.myth: Red dragon couples with sleeping mountain woman
Red dragon.note: A red dragon encountered in a dream fathers Kintoki.

Rika.note: Some derivative traditions name Seimei's otherwise unnamed wife Rika.

Sakata Kinpira.note: Kintoki is made the father of Sakata Kinpira in puppet-drama cycles.

Sao-netsu-hiko.myth: Sea voyage and Mount Kagu clay mission
Sao-netsu-hiko.note: He pilots Jimmu's expedition and later obtains sacred clay in disguise.

Satō Tadanobu.note: Benkei and Tadanobu jointly appear as Yoshitsune's retainers and defenders.

Satō Tsugunobu.note: Benkei and Tsugunobu appear as fellow Yoshitsune retainers without a distinct bilateral encounter.

Seven children.note: The stellar children greet Urashima and identify him as Kame-hime’s husband.

Shiotsutsu-no-oji.myth: Decision to undertake the eastern expedition
Shiotsutsu-no-oji.note: He tells Jimmu of the fine eastern land and its heavenly descendant.

Shizuka Gozen.note: Benkei persuades Shizuka to separate from Yoshitsune before the sea voyage.
A tearful Benkei appeals to Shizuka to mediate for him.

Shuten-dōji.note: Later versions credit Seimei with divining the oni's hiding place for Yorimitsu.
Kintoki enters disguised and participates in tricking and incapacitating the oni.
Kintoki fights in the expedition, though Yorimitsu normally delivers the decisive blow.

Soko-tsutsu-no-o.note: The Sumiyoshi god provides oracle and expeditionary protection, then receives worship.

Sukuna-bikona.note: Later interpretation tentatively identifies the song's Sukuna-mikami with Sukuna-bikona.

Sukuna-mikami.note: Jingū credits the small deity with bringing sacred liquor for Ōjin.

Sumiyoshi Myōjin.myth: Miraculous birth after his parents’ prayer
Sumiyoshi Myōjin.note: Sumiyoshi grants his parents’ request for a child and fulfills the promise through his prosperity.
Sumiyoshi Myōjin appears in disguise and assists Kintoki’s expedition.

Suruga Jirō.note: Suruga mocks or quarrels with Benkei over his carpenter-like assortment of tools.

Suzuki Saburō.note: Suzuki arrives for the final defense and fights alongside Benkei.

Sōjōbō.note: The Kurama tengu trains young Yoshitsune and predicts his future victory.

Tabura-tsu-hime.note: Jingū puts the female tsuchigumo ruler to death.

Tagishimimi.note: Tagishimimi is Jimmu's son by Ahiratsu-hime.

Taira no Masakado.note: Hidesato and Sadamori’s coalition defeated Masakado’s forces in 940.
Hidesato feigned service, learned how to distinguish the true Masakado, and exposed him.
Later romance makes Hidesato shoot Masakado’s vulnerable temple after identifying him among six doubles.

Taira no Tomomori.note: Benkei confronts Tomomori's ghost and drives it beneath the waves with prayer.
Tomomori’s ghost attacks Yoshitsune at sea before Benkei repels it by prayer.

Taizan Fukun.note: Seimei invokes Taizan Fukun for longevity, prosperity, rank, and protection.
Seimei mediates a disciple's lifespan substitution through Taizan Fukun's underworld bureaucracy.

Takagi-no-kami.note: Takagi sends Yatagarasu to guide Jimmu in the Kojiki.
Jimmu appoints Michi-no-omi to oversee public worship of Takamimusubi.

Takakuraji.myth: Divine sword revives Jimmu's army at Kumano
Takakuraji.note: He delivers the dream-disclosed heavenly sword that revives Jimmu and his force.

Takefurukuma.note: Jingū's commander defeats Oshikuma's forces through feigned surrender.

Takemiko.note: Takemiko is his child by Kibi no Anato no Takehime.

Takeuchi no Sukune.note: He assists Jingū's divination, guards Ōjin and commands against Oshikuma.

Tamamo-no-Mae.note: Popular conflations make Seimei expose her fox nature, replacing his descendant Yasuchika.

Tanzō.note: Local Tanabe tradition substitutes the historical Kumano bettō Tanzō as Benkei's father.

Togashi no Saemon.note: Benkei deceives Togashi with a blank-scroll reading and ascetic knowledge; Togashi permits the party through.

Torishikaya.note: The disguised prince drinks beside the unsuspecting Kumaso chieftain.
Yamato Takeru stabs the chieftain in the chest.
The dying chieftain bestows the title Yamato Takeru.

Tosabō Shōshun.note: Benkei joins the retainers who defeat Yoritomo's assassin and brings the captive before Yoshitsune.

Towokiwake.note: Towokiwake is his child by Kibi no Anato no Takehime.

Tsuchigumo.note: Later recensions and Edo images place Kintoki in battle against the monster.

Tsuki-sakaki-idzu-no-mitama-amazakuru-Mu.note: The Ise deity answers Jingū's divination and declares her identity.

Umashimaji.myth: Mononobe ritual service at Jimmu's court
Umashimaji.note: Later tradition magnifies Nigihayahi's son's ritual relationship to Jimmu's court.

Ura.note: Okayama discourse casts Ura as Momotarō's oni enemy through the Kibitsuhiko identification.
Ura.source: Kahara, Formation of a Regional Image

Urashima Myōjin.note: Urashima is worshipped under this divine identity after his transformation.

Usatsuhiko.myth: Reception of the expedition at Usa
Usatsuhiko.note: He receives and feeds Jimmu's party.

Usatsuhime.myth: Reception of the expedition at Usa
Usatsuhime.note: She receives Jimmu's expedition with Usatsuhiko.

Uwa-tsutsu-no-o.note: The Sumiyoshi god speaks through Jingū, supports her campaign and requests worship.

Wakatake.note: Wakatake is his child by Futaji-irihime.

Wakatakehiko.note: Wakatakehiko is his son by Ototachibanahime.

White dog of Shinano.note: The mysteriously appearing white dog guides him out of the mountain.

Wind God.note: The Wind God raises the favorable wind carrying Jingū's fleet.

Woman transformed from the great turtle.note: The captured turtle becomes a woman, accompanies Urashimako, and takes him into the sea.

Yaegiri.note: Yaegiri becomes a mountain woman and gives birth to Kintoki.

Yamatohime no Mikoto.note: Yamatohime lends him women’s clothing used to infiltrate the Kumaso feast.
Yamatohime gives him Kusanagi; Kojiki also gives an emergency bag.

Yamauba.myth: Yamauba offers her child to Yorimitsu
Yamauba.note: An unnamed yamauba presents Kintoki to Yorimitsu at Ashigara.

Yamauba.myth: Ogress brings forth the prodigious youth
Yamauba.note: An ogress brings Kintoki to Yorimitsu, who gives him his name.

Yatagarasu.myth: Guidance from Kumano through the mountains
Yatagarasu.note: The heavenly crow guides Jimmu and, in the expanded chronicle, carries messages to enemies.

eighty tailed earth-spiders.myth: Defeat of the earth-spiders in an Osaka cave
eighty tailed earth-spiders.note: Jimmu's forces defeat the cave-dwelling group described derogatorily as earth-spiders.

lunar company.myth: The lunar company retrieves Kaguya from earth
lunar company.note: The celestial collective arrives in overwhelming light, neutralizes human resistance, and carries Kaguya back to the Moon.

the golden kite.note: It alights on Jimmu's bow and blinds the hostile army with radiance.

Ōkamuzumi-no-mikoto.note: The shrine represents Momotarō as a manifestation of the divine peach.

Ōkume-no-Mikoto.note: The warrior-retainer confronts Ukashi and mediates Jimmu's courtship of Isukeyori-hime.

Ōmiwa deity.note: Jingū honors the deity's shrine with sword and spear, enabling troop assembly.

Ōmononushi.note: In the Kojiki, he is the divine father of Jimmu's queen Isukeyori-hime.

Ōtomo no Takehi.note: Ōtomo no Takehi accompanies Yamato Takeru on the eastern campaign.

Ōusu no Mikoto.note: Ōusu is Yamato Takeru’s elder or twin brother.
Ousu crushes, dismembers, wraps, and discards his brother’s body.
